headline: Colorado: Wana recalls 15 gummy batches over child-resistant packs
dek: Wana recalled 15 batches of 100 mg gummies sold at 270 Colorado stores from 19 October to 17 November after a retailer flagged faulty child-resistant packs.
key_points: Mile High Products, which trades as Wana, started a voluntary recall of 15 production batches of 100 mg gummies after a retailer spotted packs whose child-resistant features may not work.
The batches were sold at 270 Colorado stores between 19 October and 17 November, according to the Colorado Department of Revenue.
Regulators said there were no reports of adverse health events and no problem with the product itself; the defect is in the packaging.
It is the latest in a run of state recalls this autumn, from pesticide-tainted vapes in Oregon to gummies in Michigan.
body: Wana, one of the best-known edible brands in the United States, has recalled 15 batches of its 100-milligram gummies in Colorado because some packs may not be child-resistant. The Colorado Department of Revenue announced the recall on 23 November in coordination with Mile High Products LLC, the licensee that does business as Wana. The products were sold between 19 October and 17 November at 270 stores, according to the department.

The recall is about the packaging, not the gummies. The department said no issues had been found with the regulated product itself and that its Marijuana Enforcement Division (MED) had received no reports of adverse health events at the time of publication. But a pack that does not lock properly removes the main barrier between a high-dose edible and a child, which is why Colorado requires child-resistant packaging in the first place.

The problem surfaced at the shelf, not in the factory. According to the department's notice, a retailer alerted Wana to the packaging deficiency while taking in select 100-milligram gummy products. The company believes a limited number of units are affected but chose to recall every potentially affected batch so it can inspect the remaining inventory.

All 15 batches came from the same manufacturing licence, 404R-00099. They cover much of the brand's range: Stay Asleep Dreamberry and Fast Asleep Grape gummies with THC, CBG and CBN in equal parts; Relaxed Raspberry, Peaceful Pear, Colorado Sunrise and Paradise POG 20-packs; Indica, Sativa and Hybrid Assorted 10-packs; and CBD-heavy ratio products such as Serene Yuzu at 2:1 CBD to THC and Chill Black Cherry at 5:1. Two batches each of Stay Asleep Dreamberry and Peaceful Pear are included.

The department's guidance is practical. Consumers holding an affected product can throw it away or return it to the store where they bought it for disposal. Until then, the department said, they should not rely on the packaging as child-resistant and should keep the product stored securely out of children's reach. It asked anyone who suspects a child has eaten the product to seek medical attention and to report the event to the MED through its reporting form. The batch numbers and licence number printed on each label are how buyers can tell whether their pack is covered.
> A recall that starts with a store clerk noticing a loose lid is the system working. The cost lands on brands that rely on outside packaging suppliers.
## Why packaging recalls matter to operators

For a multi-state brand, a packaging fault is a supply-chain problem, not a one-off. Child-resistant closures are usually bought in from specialist suppliers, and a defect in one run can reach every product line that uses the same component, which is why a single retailer's complaint here turned into 15 batches across ratio, sleep and strain-assorted products. Retail partners bear the handling cost too: 270 stores have to pull stock, process returns and document disposal.

The department described its release as an informational notification for regulated marijuana products, and stressed that the licensee itself initiated the recall. Wana chose to recall every potentially affected batch rather than only the units found faulty, which widens the cost but narrows the risk of a defective pack staying on a shelf.
## Part of a busy recall season

Colorado's notice lands in a crowded month for product-safety actions. In Oregon, regulators recalled vapes and edibles over the pesticide bifenthrin, as we reported on 24 November. In Michigan, the Cannabis Regulatory Agency announced a voluntary recall of Gummie Joint's 'Naked Hippie - Lucky Berry' gummies produced last year after complaints that they caused an unpleasant high and possible digestive distress, according to Dentons' client alert for the week of 23 November. Colorado's MED, the same alert noted, also issued a compliance tip on vaporizer cartridges and pens, flagging what inspectors will check on ingredients, expiry dates, inventory tracking, labelling and testing.

Each of these is small on its own. Together, they show state regulators leaning harder on quality and packaging at the same time as federal rules tighten around medical cannabis and hemp. For brands, the paper trail from component supplier to batch record is becoming as important as the product formula.

Watch the MED's health and safety advisories for any update on how many units proved defective once inventory is inspected, and for any follow-up action if adverse events are reported. Watch also whether Wana or its packaging supplier discloses the cause, and whether the same closures were used on products outside the recalled batches. Finally, watch whether other retailers report similar faults at intake.
